Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Aisha Shah was thirty-two, unmarried, and had built much of her adult life around public service as a city council member in a large American city. She had been in a downtown municipal building on an ordinary weekday afternoon when the man-made disaster occurred: a sudden, coordinated attack on the public transit hub adjacent to the council offices sent smoke, alarms, shouting, and a wave of panic through the block. Aisha remembered the scene in fragments that still felt immediate to her. One moment she was moving through a corridor on her way to a meeting, hearing staff members speak over one another about evacuation, and the next she was outside with the crowd, trying to orient herself while sirens closed in and people pushed hard in every direction. What stayed with her most was not a single graphic image but the sense that the city she had taken for granted had become unpredictable in a matter of minutes. Even now, when she described it, she spoke as if the day had only recently happened, and she was careful to say that she had never again felt fully certain in a public place.

In the weeks that followed, Aisha noticed she was constantly checking her surroundings. On the elevator at city hall, she found herself standing near the doors and watching other passengers’ hands, bags, and faces instead of joining the conversation. When she entered a meeting room, she quickly chose a seat that gave her a clear view of the exits, and if that was not possible she remained uneasy until she could identify another way out. She came to feel that she always needed an escape route before she could settle anywhere, whether she was in a council chamber, a restaurant, or a friend’s apartment. If she could not map the exits, she would say she felt “stuck,” a word she used with visible tension, as though staying in the room required an effort of will. Unfamiliar places became especially difficult. Invitations to new venues, neighborhood events, and community forums that had once seemed routine began to feel unmanageable because she could not assess the danger there. Over time she declined more of them, telling colleagues she was overcommitted, even when the real issue was that she did not trust herself to relax in a place she had not already studied.

Her work environment kept putting these fears in front of her. As a council member, Aisha spent long days moving between public hearings, constituent meetings, and civic events held in different parts of the city. She had once liked that variety, but now every unfamiliar building required a private calculation about doors, crowds, and how quickly she could leave if something happened. She often arrived early so she could walk the space, and she was known among staff for standing near hallways rather than sitting at the center of a room. At night, the sense of danger sharpened. She found it harder to feel safe after dark than during the day and would remain awake in her apartment with the lights on, listening to sounds in the building and repeatedly checking the windows and locks. She was especially wary on evenings when she had been at late meetings, because the quiet streets and dim parking lots made her feel more exposed, as if the city itself had the capacity to turn without warning. Even routine trips home became occasions for vigilance, and she would scan sidewalks, parked cars, and anyone walking behind her with a seriousness that felt to her entirely necessary.

Aisha also began avoiding situations that put her body under stress. She had stopped taking the stairs when she could choose an elevator, and she was careful to pace herself because a racing heart or shortness of breath made her feel too physically vulnerable, too aware of her own body as a thing that could fail her in a crisis. She did not describe this as fear of exertion so much as a refusal to be in a state where she might not respond quickly enough if trouble appeared. That belief fit with how she understood the world now. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, that she had to be on guard all the time, and that she needed to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. These were not abstract thoughts for her; they were the instructions she lived by when she entered a building, crossed a street, sat down in a meeting, or tried to fall asleep.

By the time she sought help, the strain was showing in her daily life and in her work relationships. She had become increasingly isolated from the spontaneous parts of civic life that had once made the job meaningful to her, and she was tired of arranging her days around safety checks and exits. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was spending more time scanning for danger than actually participating in the city she had been elected to serve. She said she was not looking to become reckless, only to stop feeling as though every place might conceal the next disaster. More than anything, Aisha hoped to feel safe enough to move through her own city without constantly preparing to flee.
